prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints make credit and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks into persistent economic fluctuations

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) identified a mechanism that is simple, general and has lasted: when borrowing is limited by the value of collateral, asset prices and credit limits feed on each other, so small shocks become large and persistent. This is a conceptual advance, not a method or a measurement exercise. It is now standard in macroeconomics, in the analysis of balance-sheet channels and crises, and in models used for policy. It is also used in corporate finance, where collateral and financing constraints drive investment. I treat that last point as breadth of use, not as evidence of merit. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: the originating paper has two authors, and every member who proposed laureates for B040 named the same pair. The work is nearly three decades old, so there has been time for extension, critique and use in policy models, including after 2008. Under the common criteria it combines a foundational idea, wide influence and maturity better than any other candidate I have reviewed.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is subject overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, and with the earlier recognition of Bernanke on the financial accelerator. The committee may think financial frictions have already been recognised. A second concern is that the contribution rests heavily on one seminal paper and its extensions. Direct empirical identification of the amplification mechanism is more mixed than the theory's influence suggests. A two-person award also leaves out Gertler and Gilchrist, whose financial-accelerator and empirical work is a related but distinct strand.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B040 first and prefers the two-person Kiyotaki-Moore attribution. He flags that the 2022 prize overlaps with the subject and that empirical validation is more mixed than the theory's influence.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution and share the concern about overlap. I think the overlap is narrower than it looks. The 2022 prize recognised banks' role in crises and the analysis of bank runs. Kiyotaki-Moore concerns how collateral values and asset prices propagate shocks through the real economy. I do not think the citation should claim more than the mechanism. Validation is where I would press hardest: the committee should say that the prize recognises the theoretical mechanism and its influence on how crises are modelled, not that its quantitative size is settled.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B044 first with Autor, Katz and Hanson. She argues that the task and skill-bias strand and the trade-shock strand are both prize-worthy, but that three names omit Dorn and the task-model co-authors.
responses.response: I rank B044 second and take its scientific merit seriously. The evidence is transparent and the policy impact is large. My difficulty is attribution. Combining Katz's skill-bias work, the task framework and the China-shock papers into one prize leaves out Dorn, Levy, Murnane and Acemoglu, who is already a laureate. The B044 proposals vary on the name set, and I think that instability is a real cost. B040 does not have this problem. If the committee prefers B044, I would want it limited to the trade-shock and local-labour-market contribution, with a citation that does not imply the whole technology-and-inequality literature.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B002 first because population-scale administrative data changed how mobility and neighbourhood effects are measured. He also concedes that the durability of some estimates is still being tested.
responses.response: I agree on the importance and policy reach of the mobility work, and I ranked B002 fourth. Your own maturity caveat is what keeps it below B040 for me. Core results date from 2014 onward, long-run replication and causal interpretation of place effects are still being tested, and credit is spread across a large team with four credited names and a three-name cap. B040 has none of those problems. I do not see it as a case of favouring the old over the new. Maturity and clean attribution are common criteria, and on those B002 is not yet equal to B040. I would revisit it in a later year.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee should give to the overlap with the 2022 banking-crisis prize and Bernanke's earlier recognition on the financial accelerator.
Whether adding Gertler or Gilchrist for the financial-accelerator strand would improve or dilute the attribution.

Whether the committee prefers a single-achievement prize or a two-part prize combining B040 with another candidate. I have not found a second part that meets the maturity and attribution standard of B040.
The size of the quantitative amplification effect is not settled empirically. My assessment draws on the supplied opening statements and general knowledge, not independent verification.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My co-authors (mainly Kaplan, plus Axelson, Weisbach, Jenkinson, Lerner and others) are not credited on B040, and I see no institutional tie to Kiyotaki or Moore. My Chicago Booth adjunct post, KVA vice presidency and Stockholm-based roles do not link to the preferred or alternative candidates as far as I can tell.
